title: Healthcare AI is moving into routine diagnostic work faster than trust is generalizing across clinical tasks
source_unit: Ipsos, The AI Trust Deficit in Healthcare 2026
geography: Healthcare professionals and patients; public report summary with geography and full sample details not disclosed

observations.period: 2026; clinician adoption of AI diagnostic tools

denominator.unit: Healthcare professionals surveyed by Ipsos; public summary does not disclose the sample size or country composition

weekly_ai_diagnostic_use.unit: percent of surveyed healthcare professionals already using AI diagnostic tools weekly

adoption_stage.value: AI-enabled diagnostic tools are becoming part of everyday healthcare

observations.method: Ipsos healthcare report surveying healthcare professionals and patients about AI-powered diagnostics.
observations.uncertainty: The public summary does not identify specialties, countries, tool types, frequency thresholds or whether use is clinician-initiated, institutionally required or experimental.
observations.subgroup: Healthcare professionals surveyed in the Ipsos study.
observations.counterinterpretation: Weekly use may reflect workflow exposure rather than confidence in autonomous diagnosis; clinicians can use AI as a checking or triage layer while retaining human responsibility.

observations.period: 2026; patient awareness of AI in diagnostics

denominator.unit: Patients surveyed by Ipsos; public summary does not disclose the sample size or country composition

patient_ai_diagnostic_awareness.unit: percent of surveyed patients with at least some awareness of AI in diagnostics

awareness_adoption_gap.unit: percentage-point difference between patient awareness and weekly clinician use; descriptive, not a population gap estimate

observations.method: Ipsos comparison of patient awareness and healthcare-professional use within the AI diagnostic study.
observations.uncertainty: Awareness does not indicate informed consent, perceived benefit, actual exposure to AI in care or ability to distinguish assistive from autonomous systems.
observations.subgroup: Patients surveyed in the Ipsos study.
observations.counterinterpretation: High awareness may be driven by public discussion rather than personal clinical encounters; it can still create expectations that providers need to explain and manage.

denominator.unit: Patients and healthcare professionals in the Ipsos study; application-specific denominators and shares not disclosed on the public summary

higher_trust_tasks.value: Trust is highest in lower-friction applications such as cancer screening and blood-test analysis

lower_trust_tasks.value: Trust is lower in mental-health assessment and surgical guidance

trust_gradient.value: Confidence varies by perceived stakes, interpretability, human contact and tolerance for error rather than by AI label alone
trust_gradient.unit: analytical interpretation grounded in the reported task contrast

observations.method: Task-level comparison of confidence in AI-powered diagnostic applications.
observations.uncertainty: The public summary does not provide application-level percentages or test whether trust differences arise from risk, explainability, stigma, clinician relationship or familiarity.
observations.subgroup: Patients and healthcare professionals included in the study.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower trust in mental-health assessment or surgical guidance may indicate appropriate caution about high-context tasks rather than a general deficit that more marketing can solve.

related_sources.claim: Official Ipsos landing page for the full report; download requires registration.
Official Ipsos healthcare topic page contextualizing the report among current health research.

boundary: This record adds a clinical-trust mechanism: healthcare AI adoption and patient awareness can advance while confidence remains task-specific, with higher acceptance in lower-friction analytic applications and lower acceptance where judgment, vulnerability and consequence are harder to separate from the human relationship. It is a public summary of a healthcare opinion study, not a clinical validation, safety assessment, implementation evaluation or patient-outcome dataset.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Ipsos report summary, gated report landing page and healthcare topic page were retrieved and reviewed for clinician use, patient awareness and task-specific trust; the public summary page was hashed.
